briefing: Trump says the U.S. could strike Iran as soon as tomorrow unless Tehran makes a deal, after Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and oil sites pushed Washington to issue travel warnings for 13 Middle East countries; Brent crude sits near US$117 ahead of Sunday night's market reopening. B.C. polls close at 11 p.m. Ontario time, and Ontarians elect mayors and councils on Monday, the same day First Nations leaders meet Carney and the premiers in Ottawa. The Bank of Canada's rate decision Wednesday and Ontario's fiscal update Thursday follow.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of nuclear talks. The first wave killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones on Israel, Gulf states and U.S. bases, and closed the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through. A peace memorandum signed in June briefly reopened shipping, but it fell apart in July when Iran started attacking commercial ships again to press its claim over the strait.
stories.headline: Trump says an Iran strike could come 'tomorrow' as Houthi attacks spread
stories.impact: This is a big part of why gas and diesel in Ontario stay expensive: GTA regular is forecast around $1.80 a litre on Friday and diesel near $2.65. Diesel feeds straight into grocery and delivery prices, and higher fuel is one reason the Bank of Canada has been cautious about cutting rates.
stories.now: Trump told reporters the U.S. could strike Iran 'tomorrow' or make a deal, saying the choice is Tehran's and that he wants a permanent end to Iran's nuclear-weapon ambitions; earlier this month he had said there would be no strike before the November 3 midterms. An outlet tied to Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tehran has made no new offer on the Strait of Hormuz and rejects swapping a Hormuz reopening for an end to the U.S. naval blockade. The State Department issued travel advisories for 13 countries, including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and Israel, and is moving some diplomats and families out of the region, while the carrier USS George Washington is reportedly loading munitions. Saudi authorities say a recent Houthi strike on Dammam's airport killed two people and injured eight, and that debris from intercepted missiles fell near Mecca and Medina, which the Houthis deny targeting. Brent crude settled Friday at US$116.72, its highest since March, and trading resumes Sunday evening.

stories.backstory: Eby's NDP won a one-seat majority in October 2024, just ahead of a Conservative party that had surged from almost nowhere. On September 22, 2026, Eby called an election two years early, while the Conservatives had only just chosen a new leader, which critics said was unfair. Days before the call, eight Conservative members had broken away to form a new party, CentreBC, though seven later returned. Lorne Doerkson now leads the Conservatives, and Emily Lowan leads the Greens.
stories.headline: B.C. polls close at 11 p.m. Ontario time with Conservatives narrowly ahead
stories.impact: Day-to-day life in Ontario won't change much, but a new B.C. government could take different positions on pipelines, carbon pricing and trade that affect national deals Ontario is part of.
stories.now: Voting runs until 8 p.m. Pacific time (11 p.m. in Ontario); advance and district-office paper ballots are counted electronically and will be reported first, while election-day ballots are counted by hand, and mail-in ballots take about two weeks, so close seats may stay undecided. Advance turnout was 891,348, about 6.5% lower than the 953,025 who voted early in 2024. NDP Premier David Eby voted Saturday morning with his family, while Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan voted in advance. The final Ipsos poll for Global News had the Conservatives at 44%, the NDP at 39% and the Greens at 13%. The legislature has 93 seats, so 47 are needed for a majority.

stories.backstory: Chow won a 2023 by-election after John Tory resigned and is now seeking a full term. Bradford, a councillor, is her main challenger. Late-summer polls had Chow around 50% and Bradford near 39%. Big themes are housing costs, traffic, property taxes and the province's moves on bike lanes.
stories.headline: Chow and Bradford make final weekend push before Monday's vote
stories.impact: You get a vote for mayor, ward councillor and school trustee in your own city. Check your municipality's site for your polling station and advance-voting hours.
stories.now: On Saturday Bradford argued the city is ready for a change while Chow urged supporters to turn out, capping a final week in which Bradford toured all 25 wards promising a first-year property-tax freeze, 1,000 more police officers and a 25% cut to water bills. Liaison Strategies (49% to 47%) and Mainstreet Research (48.9% to 47.5%) have Bradford narrowly ahead, while Nanos for CP24 and CTV (49.8% to 46.6%) and Pollara (53% to 46%) have Chow in front. Advance turnout hit 222,550, the most in at least 16 years and nearly double 2022's 115,911. Polls open Monday from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. in Toronto, and Mississauga, Brampton, York Region and the rest of Ontario vote the same day.

stories.backstory: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad emergency tariffs in February, but sector tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, copper and lumber stayed. At the first CUSMA review on July 1, the U.S. refused to extend the deal for a full new term, so it now needs annual reviews. Ottawa walked out of talks on August 21, calling Washington's last-minute demands unfair. The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on August 22, and Canada matched with counter-tariffs on September 8, plus a $25B support package for affected workers and businesses.
stories.headline: U.S. reshuffles which Canadian goods face 50% tariffs
stories.impact: Canadian makers of flooring, carpets and personal-care products shipping to the U.S. face new 50% duties from month's end, which could hit some GTA manufacturers and their jobs. For most tariffed goods, little changes, and prices on U.S. goods hit by Canada's counter-tariffs stay elevated.
stories.now: Items coming off the list include seaweed, packing boxes and some plywood sheets, while cocoa powder, vinyl flooring, shampoos and carpets are being added; the changes take effect at the end of October. Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins, who faces a tough re-election fight, said she pushed for exemptions for her state's farm and seaweed producers. Trade lawyers note more goods are being added than removed, so the net relief is small, and analysts see the move as largely political ahead of November 3. Trump said a deal is not done but Canada is working hard on it, while Carney said Canada would sign quickly once Washington is ready. Ottawa says it is reviewing the changes, and its counter-tariffs on about C$27.6 billion of U.S. goods stay in place.

stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war closed much of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, and fuel costs have fed through to inflation since. Brent fell to about $74 in late June when shipping recovered, then climbed again as attacks resumed this autumn. Canada's central bank has weighed whether an energy-driven spike is temporary or will spread to other prices.
stories.headline: Retail sales rebound as markets bet on a Bank of Canada hike
stories.impact: Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit would cost more within days of a hike, and anyone renewing a GTA mortgage this fall should test their budget at a higher rate. High pump prices will keep squeezing commuters either way.
stories.now: Statistics Canada's Friday report showed retail sales up about 1.2% in August, slightly below the 1.3% economists expected, with sales excluding autos also up 1.2%; that follows a 0.7% drop in July, and the agency's early estimate points to another 0.7% gain in September. Earlier this week, September inflation came in at 3.1%, driven by a 27.8% jump in gasoline prices, though inflation excluding gasoline was only 2.2% and the bank's core measures averaged about 1.9%. Swap markets have priced roughly an 80% or higher chance of a quarter-point hike to 2.50% next Wednesday, and BMO, RBC, Desjardins and Scotiabank now call for one. Arguing against a hike, Canada lost 68,000 jobs in September and unemployment rose to 6.5%. The loonie is holding near 71 U.S. cents, close to a four-week high. Friday's oil jump above US$116 adds to the pressure on gasoline prices.

stories.backstory: Republicans have controlled both the House and Senate since January 2025, which has let Trump pass his agenda with few checks. Midterms usually go against the president's party, and Trump's approval is lower than at the same point in his first term. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot. A Democratic House could launch investigations and block spending and trade legislation.
stories.headline: Trump rallies in Georgia as Obama calls the Iran war unnecessary
stories.impact: A change in Congress could shift the odds of tariff relief for Ontario's auto, steel and lumber industries. Ottawa's trade strategy is partly being timed around the outcome.
stories.now: Trump's rally at the Georgia National Fairgrounds in Perry backed Rep. Mike Collins, the Republican Senate nominee, and governor candidate Rick Jackson, and he heads to Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday. Obama campaigned in Cleveland for Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, then in Michigan for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, telling the crowd the Iran war was unnecessary and had left Tehran with effective control over the Strait of Hormuz. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report estimates Democrats will gain 12 to 22 House seats, more than they need for control, and rates seven Senate races as toss-ups. The Associated Press counts more than 20 million early ballots, and gas prices remain a central issue, with the AAA national average at US$4.29 a gallon versus $3.07 a year ago.

stories.backstory: Peltola, a former one-term congresswoman, topped the August nonpartisan primary and is in a close race with Sullivan. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so voters can rank both Sullivans if they are unsure. Democrats and voting-rights groups have long warned the administration might try to stop states from certifying races Trump's party loses. Under the Constitution, states run their own elections within rules set by Congress.
stories.headline: Justice Department sues to block a possible Democratic win in Alaska
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario, but a fight over who controls the U.S. Senate would shape how much room Trump has on tariffs against Canada next year.
stories.now: The U.S. Justice Department filed the suit in federal court in Alaska, 11 days before the November 3 vote, and Trump said he ordered it. It targets Daniel J. Sullivan of Petersburg, who appears on the ballot with no party label and drew 4,107 votes (about 2%) in the August primary, versus more than 68,000 for the incumbent. The suit also asks for a probe into whether votes for him were meant for the senator; Republicans call him a Democratic plant, which he denies, and Alaska's Supreme Court already refused to remove him. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department does not aim to interfere improperly, while Democrats called it a sham, and a Notre Dame election-law expert said the statute does not appear to allow blocking certification.

stories.backstory: The Parliamentary Budget Officer is an independent officer of Parliament who checks the government's fiscal numbers. The Carney government split its books into operating and capital budgets in 2025, arguing that borrowing to build things like ports, pipelines and housing is different from borrowing for day-to-day costs. Critics say the split makes overall deficits look smaller than they are. The 50% U.S. tariffs imposed in August have slowed growth and cut into federal revenue.
stories.headline: Budget watchdog warns of rising federal debt before Nov. 5 budget
stories.impact: Higher federal borrowing can keep upward pressure on bond yields, which feed into fixed mortgage rates for GTA homeowners. Watch the budget for changes to tariff relief, housing programs and any tax measures.
stories.now: In an interview for CTV's Question Period, Ryan said debt-servicing costs are now the fastest-growing part of federal spending and that her office projects the debt-to-GDP ratio rising over the next few years. Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised to balance the operating budget, which excludes capital investment, by 2027-28, a year earlier than first planned; Ryan's outlook has that happening a year later. She said the deficit looks slightly better this year but worsens over five years, and flagged about $400 billion being routed through Crown corporations, loans and special funds that get less scrutiny from Parliament. Her office's outlook, released this week, also lowers its growth forecast because of the U.S. tariff war. Carney returns to Ottawa Saturday from Turkey, where he and President Erdogan agreed to a strategic partnership and to start free-trade talks.

stories.backstory: Cleveland-Cliffs, an Ohio steelmaker, bought Hamilton-based Stelco in 2024, and Ottawa approved the deal on condition that union jobs and most non-union roles be kept. U.S. 50% tariffs on Canadian steel since August have hit exports hard. In early October Stelco announced a partial shutdown of finishing lines at Hamilton Works, cutting up to 500 jobs, and Joly gave the company five days to respond. The dispute has become a test of whether Ottawa can enforce foreign-takeover promises.
stories.headline: Ottawa gives Stelco owner 15 days to reverse layoffs
stories.impact: Hundreds of Hamilton families face lost paycheques, with knock-on effects for suppliers and the local economy. The outcome may shape whether the new federal-Ontario steel fund keeps similar plants running.
stories.now: In a letter sent Thursday, Joly gave Cleveland-Cliffs 15 days to meet the job commitments it made when it bought Stelco in 2024, or face court action. She says Ottawa has found a breach and that a forced sale is on the table, adding that some potential buyers have shown interest. Up to 500 jobs at the Hamilton and Lake Erie operations are affected, and about 200 workers have already been laid off. Cleveland-Cliffs, which blames 50% U.S. tariffs and low steel prices, has not commented on the letter, while Premier Doug Ford and the steelworkers' union back Ottawa.

stories.backstory: The spring 2026 budget pushed Ontario's target for balancing the books back to 2028-29. U.S. tariffs of up to 50% on Canadian goods have hit the province's steel, auto and lumber industries hardest. Fall economic statements update the budget's numbers and often add targeted tax or spending changes. This week Ottawa and Ontario announced an $8.7-billion plan for steel, autos and Ring of Fire roads.
stories.headline: Ontario to table its fall fiscal update on Thursday
stories.impact: Watch for changes affecting OSAP, health and education funding, gas taxes or tariff relief for workers; any tighter spending could show up in public services across the GTA.
stories.now: Bethlenfalvy announced the October 29 date in a Canadian Club speech in Toronto, two days after Queen's Park returns from its 21-week break. Ontario ended 2025-26 with a deficit of about $13 billion, and he said this year's will be higher, in line with the spring budget's $13.8-billion forecast. He said the province has handled U.S. tariffs better than economists expected but that slower growth is driving the red ink. He gave no details on new measures beyond a focused, responsible spending approach.

stories.backstory: Teacher and education-worker contracts in Ontario are bargained centrally with the province. The Ford government has taken more direct control of several school boards, citing deficits and governance problems, and passed legislation expanding the education minister's powers. The government says per-student funding is at a record high in dollar terms; the unions and the Financial Accountability Office say it has fallen once inflation is counted.
stories.headline: Education unions rally in five Ontario cities over school funding
stories.impact: Parents in the GTA should watch bargaining updates for any strike votes. Monday's ballot includes school trustees, who now have less power but still represent families to the board.
stories.now: The rallies ran from 1 to 2:30 p.m. at Queen's Park in Toronto, Parliament Hill in Ottawa, and parks in London, Sudbury and Thunder Bay, led by the presidents of the secondary (OSSTF), Catholic (OECTA), elementary (ETFO) and French-language (AEFO) teachers' unions and CUPE's school board council. The unions say a $6.5-billion gap means fewer staff and supports, and cite a Financial Accountability Office finding that real per-student funding is near a 10-year low and set to fall further. They also point to class sizes, school violence, special-education supports and growing provincial control over school boards, and say Bill 101 has weakened trustees, contributing to fewer trustee candidates in Monday's elections. The rallies come as contract bargaining continues and three days before Queen's Park returns.

stories.backstory: Parental abductions happen when a parent without legal custody takes a child in breach of a court order or custody arrangement. Police in Ontario issue Amber Alerts only when they believe a child is in imminent danger, which is why many of these cases are handled through public appeals instead. Toronto police first asked for the public's help on Friday evening and widened the appeal on Saturday.
stories.headline: Toronto police hunt for mother and three young children after alleged abduction
stories.impact: Anyone in the GTA who sees the mother, the children, the person of interest or a white Ford Expedition with plate DJS 875 should call 911 rather than approach them.
stories.now: Police say Somerda Miclescu, 22, who does not have custody, took her children around 11:30 a.m. Friday during a semi-supervised visit at a relative's home near Midland and Eglinton avenues in Scarborough. The children are Anastasia, four months, Irina, 3, and Daniel, 6. On Saturday Inspector Jeff Allington named Ionut Stroe, 25, as a person of interest; his white 2017 Ford Expedition, Ontario plate DJS 875, is believed to have been used, and he is separately wanted for breaching a release order. Police say the case does not meet the threshold for an Amber Alert and they have no information that the children are in danger or being taken out of the province; anyone who sees them should call 911.

stories.backstory: Tech giants have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into data centres and chips for AI, and those stocks have driven much of the market's gains. Investors have swung between excitement and doubt about whether the spending will pay off. This year's oil shock from the Iran war has also kept inflation and interest-rate worries alive.
stories.headline: Dow sheds 653 points as oil climbs to a six-month high
stories.impact: Many Ontario RRSPs, TFSAs and pension plans hold U.S. tech through index funds, so expect a dip on statements if the selloff continues. A slightly stronger loonie makes U.S. purchases a touch cheaper.
stories.now: The Dow fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to close at 52,215.16, while the S&P 500 lost 0.52% to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq slipped 0.21% to 25,955.34. Airlines such as United, Delta and American fell on higher fuel costs, and AI cloud-computing firms like CoreWeave extended Thursday's losses, while cybersecurity stocks rose more than 7% on strong outlooks. The Dow still ended the week higher, but the S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted a second straight weekly decline. Toronto's S&P/TSX composite traded lower through the day, and the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield closed at about 4.99%. Markets widely expect the U.S. Federal Reserve to hold rates on October 28.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion is in its fifth year. Trump's envoys have made several trips to Moscow, while Zelenskyy has pushed for a leaders' meeting that Russia rejects. Russia has been pounding Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter, and Kyiv has struck Russian refineries in return. Ukraine has also complained about U.S. limits on intelligence sharing and a Starlink slowdown.
stories.headline: Russia hits Kyiv with drones as Carney warns over Starlink
stories.impact: Canada is a major Ukraine backer and is being asked for more money at the October 29–30 Canada-EU summit, which affects federal spending. Any real progress toward peace could ease diesel and gas prices over time.
stories.now: Russia launched 126 drones overnight, 61 of them jet-powered, and Ukraine says it downed 101; one hit a residential building in Kyiv's Obolon district, injuring two and starting a fire. Over the past day 4 people were killed and 78 injured across Ukraine, including in Chernihiv, Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and Dnipro. In Istanbul on Friday, Carney said the slowdown of SpaceX's military satellite service had caused casualties and that Canada should not rely on one provider a single country can pressure. Putin says any deal must be a final settlement rather than a temporary truce, while the White House says a local ceasefire in occupied Oleshky starts October 29 and the Kremlin says three-way talks resume next month.

stories.why: It is the first concrete sign in weeks that direct talks could restart, but both sides are still escalating strikes, and Moscow continues to demand all of Donetsk and no NATO membership for Kyiv. Moscow's offer to help on Iran also links the two wars driving energy prices.
